rationale: A wins because it keeps the dangerous word "profitable" on a leash: "Peloton posts its first profitable quarter in three years — on adjusted EBITDA, not net income" is the honest version of the story. B has real angles, but "Peloton is calling itself profitable. Its own numbers disagree." turns a qualified accounting distinction into a gotcha it cannot fully prove from the update. A is less cute and more useful, which is usually how press gets landed.
gaps_in_A: "Peloton is selling bikes by the month now — the hardware company is becoming a subscription company" overstates the identity shift; Peloton already has a membership business, so the real question is whether rentals change hardware economics.

"Peloton's subscriber churn just hit a record low — the retention problem may be the one that's actually fixed" leans toward a solved-problem narrative without the actual churn rate, baseline, or cause.

"consumer-discretionary or fitness-industry markets reporter at a business outlet" is acceptable, but still a touch broad; the strongest version would name the earnings/retail-subscription lane more tightly.
gaps_in_B: "How Peloton's new CEO manufactured its first profitable quarter in three years" implies causation and artificial construction; the update says costs were cut and EBITDA/FCF turned positive, not that the CEO single-handedly manufactured the quarter.

"Peloton is calling itself profitable. Its own numbers disagree." invents a sharper company claim than the update gives and makes adjusted EBITDA/FCF sound like fake numbers rather than different metrics.
"after three straight years without it" is a loose rewrite of "first profitable quarter in three years" and needs the actual comparable quarter to avoid mushy chronology.
"Next step: `find-journalists`" is early. Pick the angle, lock the proof, then fit-check journalists; otherwise you build a list around headlines that may not survive diligence.
